fixes.explanation: Three thousand it is. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" and goes looking for David and his men (1 Samuel 24:2). That's a LOT of sandals on one dusty road. All that marching just to find David.

The text doesn't put anybody from Keilah in this scene. It says "…David and his men were hiding in the recesses of the cave." (1 Samuel 24:3). Saul went in to relieve himself, and the cave already had company in the back. I bet he came in expecting a quiet moment.

Enemy is right. David's men tell him, "This is the day about which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand…’" (1 Samuel 24:4). Then they urge David toward Saul. I think they were ready to start the celebration.

A kingdom is a big gift, but it isn't the word in the men's quote. They say the LORD told David, "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand…" (1 Samuel 24:4). Swapping in kingdom is like tossing raisins in when the recipe calls for chocolate chips. Same batch, different ingredient.

Not people, friend. The words David's men repeat are, "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish." (1 Samuel 24:4). The LORD's words are about an enemy being handed over, and nobody else gets named. Put people in there and the whole line changes.

Not quite, friend. The text says "Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:5). He didn't feel good about it. His conscience was stricken.
False is right. "Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:5). He didn't feel good about it. That tells you a lot about David.

Servant is a fine word, and I'd happily wear it, but David doesn't use it here. He says, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). That one word is the reason he gives for holding back.

Champion sounds mighty, like a trophy on a cookie contest shelf, but David picks a different word. He says, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). Anointed is the reason he gives, plain and simple.

True. "With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul." (1 Samuel 24:7). Those men had just said it was the day, and David still held them back. He did it with his words.
That's it. "Then Saul left the cave and went on his way." (1 Samuel 24:7). He walks out while David is holding his men back. Quiet exit, and a corner of his robe is already gone (1 Samuel 24:4).

First David calls out, "My lord the king!" Then David "…bowed facedown in reverence" (1 Samuel 24:8). He greets the king who has been hunting him (1 Samuel 24:11) with a bow. That tells you what's in his heart toward Saul.

Mock is a sneaky guess, but it's not the word David uses. He asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ‘Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). The charge is that David wants to harm Saul, and he's asking why Saul listens to the men saying it.

Desert fits the wilderness setting, but it doesn't show up in David's question. He says, "Look, David intends to harm you…" (1 Samuel 24:9). Harm is what the men are accusing him of, and David is asking why Saul listens.
True. David says, "I was told to kill you, but I spared you…" (1 Samuel 24:10). He says it right to the king's face. I think that's honest about how close it got.

Rebellion is right. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). Just before that he tells Saul, "…look at the corner of your robe in my hand." So the robe corner is his proof.

Fear isn't in that sentence, though it'd be a natural guess for a man hiding in a cave. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). Evil and rebellion are the two things he says aren't in his hands.

Pride isn't the word here. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). He's answering the charge that he intends harm, so evil and rebellion are the two he names.
Those are big, scary animals, and David doesn't use them here. He asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). A dead dog and a flea are what he names. Not a lion in sight.

Saul's hand. David says, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). He's asking the LORD to plead his case. He's talking to Saul, so "your hand" is Saul's.

The Philistines don't come up in David's words here. He says, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). David is speaking to Saul, so "your hand" is Saul's.
David's men aren't named in those words. He says, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). He's speaking to Saul, so "your hand" is Saul's.
Servant isn't what Saul says. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). He calls David his son, and that comes right after David called him "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11).
Friend is a nice word, but Saul uses a different one. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David had said "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11), and Saul answers with "my son."

Saul doesn't say that. After weeping, he says, "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." (1 Samuel 24:17). He admits David has treated him with good. That's the opposite of calling David a fooler.
True. Saul says, "May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day." (1 Samuel 24:19). Those are his exact words to David. He's asking the LORD to reward David with good.

Not false, friend. Saul really does say, "May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day." (1 Samuel 24:19). He's asking the LORD to reward David with good. It's right there in the verse.
Priest is a respectable job, but Saul isn't talking about that. He says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king…" (1 Samuel 24:20). The word is king.

Judge sounds official, but it isn't what Saul says. He says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). The word is king, and the kingdom of Israel goes with it.

The Philistines don't come up in Saul's request. He asks David to swear "…that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house." (1 Samuel 24:21). It's about his family line, not a battle.
False is right. "…David gave his oath to Saul." (1 Samuel 24:22). He gave Saul what he asked for. Saul had asked for that oath in the verse before (1 Samuel 24:21).
Up to the stronghold. "…Saul returned home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). They each go their own way. Saul heads home while David and his men climb up.
Keilah isn't named here. The text says "…David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). Saul is the one heading home.
